title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, a bonfire for Prahlad and a morning of color. Your line was everyone's the same color today. Today, a night nobody sleeps.

A hunter goes into the forest and finds nothing, all day. Night falls, and he's too far from home and too stubborn to go back empty-handed. So he climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and waits. He hasn't eaten. He can't let himself sleep, or he'll fall. To keep busy, he plucks leaves off the branch, one by one, and drops them without looking where they land. This is one of the stories told on Maha Shivaratri: a man who keeps the festival perfectly without knowing it exists.
screen: `A HUNTER WITH NOTHING.` → `A TREE BESIDE A POOL.` → `LEAVES DROPPED IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Shiva-ratri: the night of Shiva. Maha: great. It falls on the fourteenth night of the waning moon, in late winter, the last dark before the new moon. The hunter's tree was a bilva, whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva. And under it, hidden in the dark, was a lingam, the simple rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples and shrines. All night his dropped leaves fell on it, and drops from his water pot spilled on it. He fasted, because he had no food. He stayed awake, because he had to. Without meaning to, he had done what Shivaratri asks: fast, keep vigil, offer water and bilva leaves to the lingam. In the Shiva Purana's telling, deer come to the pool through the night, and each one asks to be spared long enough to go home first, and the hunter, softening, lets them go. By dawn, the story says, his heart is changed, and Shiva's grace reaches him. That's what people across India do on this night, on purpose. Temples stay open until morning. Devotees pour water, milk and honey over the lingam, in a rite called abhisheka. Many repeat five syllables, na-mah shi-va-ya, Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, until the sky gets light. Different stories are given for the night: Shiva's marriage to Parvati, or the night he drank the world's poison. But the practice is the same: don't sleep through the night that matters.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI: THE GREAT NIGHT.` · `BILVA LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN LINGAM.` · `A FAST AND A VIGIL, BY ACCIDENT.` · `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA UNTIL DAWN.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, the way the hunter had to on his branch, and follow the breath. When the first urge comes to stop, to check your phone, to be done, stay for three more breaths, counting gently, and notice what's on the other side of that urge.
Shivaratri. The night of Shiva, kept awake with fasting, water and bilva leaves on the lingam, and Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. The hunter found it by accident. Good night, for now.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water or milk over the lingam with bilva leaves, and keep vigil through the night repeating Om Namah Shivaya; many temples stay open until dawn.

chat.says: How does the hunter in the Shivaratri story keep the festival without knowing it?
options: He fasts, stays awake in a bilva tree, and drops leaves and water on a hidden lingam.
He follows a group of pilgrims through the forest and copies what they do all night.
He builds a small fire under the tree and chants Shiva's name to keep warm.
chat.meaning: Without meaning to, the hunter fasted, kept vigil, and offered water and bilva leaves to the lingam: just what Shivaratri asks.
